title: Review: Current density and non-uniform conductors; Series and parallel circuits; Kirchhoff's laws; Resistance and I–V characteristics; Resistivity
qualification: AP Physics C: Electricity and Magnetism
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for AP Physics C: Electricity and Magnetism (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: EL04-1#t2 term and clue written for the game; EL06-ap1#t1 term and clue written for the game; EL03-1#t2 term and clue written for the game; NEW-current-density-calc-1#t2 term and clue written for the game. Questions: EL03-1#N.3b, EL04-1#N.9, EL06-1#N.10b, EL06-ap1#N.9, NEW-current-density-calc-1#N.5, EL03-1#N.14b, EL04-1#N.10b, EL06-1#N.11, EL06-ap1#N.8b, NEW-current-density-calc-1#N.9, EL04-1#N.6b, EL06-1#N.2. Some questions repeat from the worlds it reviews.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Resistance
items.clue: Quantity proportional to the length of a wire and to 1/A.

items.label: Loop rule
items.clue: Statement that ΣΔV = 0 around every closed path, with or without a battery.

items.label: Ohm's law
items.clue: Special case in which V/I stays constant: a straight I–V line through the origin.

items.label: Drift velocity
items.clue: Vector multiplied by n and q to give J; it describes how the charge carriers move.

questions.stem: A resistor sealed in plastic is placed in an insulated cup of water and connected to an ideal battery. While there is a steady current in the resistor, the temperature of the water rises. Which statement correctly describes where the energy that warms the water comes from?

options.text: Part of the charge that flows into the resistor is used up, becoming thermal energy.
Heat that was stored inside the battery flows along the wires with the current.
Energy the charges carry from the battery becomes thermal energy in the resistor.
The charges slow down in the resistor, and their lost kinetic energy heats it.

questions.stem: A copper wire is connected across an ideal battery. The wire is then cooled from 60 °C to 20 °C; its length and cross-sectional area change by negligible amounts. How do the wire's resistance and the current in it change as it cools?

options.text: The resistance increases, and the current decreases.
The resistance and the current both remain the same.
The resistance decreases; the current does not vary.
The resistance decreases, and the current increases.

questions.stem: A student connects an ideal voltmeter in series with a resistor of resistance R and an ideal battery of emf ε, forming a single loop. Which describes the voltmeter reading and the current in the resistor?

options.text: The reading is zero, and the current in the resistor is zero.
The reading is ε, and the current in the resistor is zero.
The reading is zero, and the current in the resistor is ε/R.
The reading is ε, and the current in the resistor is ε/R.

questions.stem: A student builds a single loop from a battery, two resistors R₁ and R₂, a switch and connecting wires. Using an ideal voltmeter, the student measures 6.0 V across the battery's terminals, 2.5 V across R₁ and 2.5 V across R₂. Which conclusion is best supported by these measurements?

options.text: The other 1.0 V was used up by the charges as they traveled all the way around the loop.
Some other part of the loop, such as the switch or a connection, has 1.0 V across it.
The battery has internal resistance, and the missing 1.0 V is dropped across that resistance.
The meter misread both resistors, which should each have 3.0 V across them.

questions.stem: A long, straight wire of radius R carries a current whose density is directed along the wire and has magnitude J(r) = J₀r/R, where r is the distance from the wire's axis and J₀ is a positive constant. What is the current in the wire?

options.text: 2πJ₀R²/3
πJ₀R²
πJ₀R²/2
J₀R²/3

questions.stem: Two components are tested. Component P: ΔV = 2.0 V, I = 0.40 A; 4.0 V, 0.80 A; 6.0 V, 1.2 A. Component Q: 2.0 V, 0.50 A; 4.0 V, 0.80 A; 6.0 V, 1.0 A. Which is ohmic over this range?

options.text: Q only, because its current is the larger at the lowest potential difference.
P only, because ΔV/I is 5.0 Ω at every reading.
Both, because the current rises whenever the potential difference rises.
Neither, because ΔV = IR gives a resistance for each reading of both.

questions.explanation: P: 2.0/0.40 = 4.0/0.80 = 6.0/1.2 = 5.0 Ω, constant, so I ∝ ΔV. Q's ratio rises from 4.0 Ω to 6.0 Ω, so Q is not ohmic.

questions.stem: Wire X has resistance R_X. Wire Y is made of the same material as X, is three times as long as X, and has twice the diameter of X. Both wires have uniform cross sections. What is the ratio R_Y/R_X?

options.text: R_Y/R_X = 12
R_Y/R_X = 1

questions.stem: Three identical lamps are connected to a supply of negligible internal resistance: lamp A is in series with lamps B and C, which are in parallel with each other. The filament of lamp C breaks. What happens to the brightness of lamps A and B? (Assume each lamp's resistance stays the same.)

options.text: A and B both go out, because the circuit is now broken.
A becomes dimmer and B becomes brighter.
A stays the same and B becomes brighter, because B now carries C's current.
A becomes brighter and B stays the same, because the parallel branch keeps its potential difference.

questions.stem: Two resistors, each of resistance R, are connected in series with an ideal battery of emf ε. A nonideal voltmeter, whose resistance is 4R, is connected across one of the resistors. What does the voltmeter read?

A long wire of length ℓ consists of a solid core of radius a and resistivity ρ, surrounded by a tightly fitting layer of a different metal, of resistivity ρ/4, that extends from r = a to r = 2a, where r is the distance from the wire's axis. Each end of the wire is attached to a thick metal plate, and the two plates are held at a potential difference ΔV. What is the current in the wire?

options.text: 17πa²ΔV/(ρℓ)
13πa²ΔV/(ρℓ)
16πa²ΔV/(ρℓ)
7πa²ρΔV/(4ℓ)

questions.stem: A student makes a resistor from nichrome wire of diameter 1.5 mm. Nichrome has a resistivity of 1.1 × 10⁻⁶ Ω·m. What length of the wire is needed for the current in it to be 2.4 A when the potential difference across it is 3.0 V?

Three circuits are each made from an identical cell of negligible internal resistance, a resistor and a lamp. In circuit 1 the three form a single closed loop. Circuit 2 is the same loop with an open switch added. Circuit 3 is the same loop as circuit 1 with a wire of negligible resistance connected directly across the lamp's terminals. Which ranks the currents I₁, I₂ and I₃ in the lamps of circuits 1, 2 and 3?

options.text: I₁ > I₂ = I₃
I₁ = I₃ > I₂
I₃ > I₁ > I₂
I₁ = I₂ = I₃
